Need to search first.Search works again. Let me look at these snippets.I've written notes on all 25 verses, but they're less complete than you asked for. Partway through, the tools hit a usage limit, so I couldn't open any page in full. Everything below comes from the excerpts my searches returned. That means I didn't get through the full verse-by-verse text of Gill, Ellicott or the Pulpit Commentary, and I found nothing for some verses. Where a page groups several authors under one link, I name the author when the excerpt did.

**Gaps:** I found no Reformed, Baptist, Methodist or Pentecostal disagreement over what this chapter means. The only place traditions clearly split is the status of the "Prayer of Manasseh" (vv. 18–19). I also found nothing from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org, and nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers.

---

### Whole chapter
- The Pulpit Commentary says the chapter keeps stressing how Manasseh and his people ignored God's word and law. It sees this as one of the writer's main aims. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- Ligonier says Chronicles was written for people back from exile, so it highlights repentance. That is why it paints Manasseh more kindly than 2 Kings 21. Kings leaves out his repentance because it wants to show how his sins made the exile certain. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/manassehs-repentance
- A Bible Hub Q&A says the two books don't contradict each other. Kings stresses how evil piled up toward judgment; Chronicles stresses restoration and repentance. https://biblehub.com/q/how_to_reconcile_manasseh's_repentance.htm

### Traditional reading

**v. 1:** Guzik (quoting Knapp) notes that Manasseh was born during the 15 extra years God gave Hezekiah. Knapp says Hezekiah would rather have died childless than have such a son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that 2 Kings gives his mother's name, Hephzibah ("my delight is in her"). Whitelaw says tradition made her Isaiah's daughter. He also reads the name Manasseh as "one who forgets," which fits a man who forgot God. He adds that Manasseh became king so young that he held the sceptre while still a pupil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- The Cambridge Bible notes that the Chronicler leaves out the mother's name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/33-1.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary calls the 55-year reign a merciful example of time given for repentance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html

**v. 2:** A source quoted on Precept Austin says grace isn't inherited: the best parents may have the worst children, and the sons of good men who turn bad are often among the worst. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-33-commentary
- Matthew Henry says Manasseh went against his father's good example and upbringing and copied the pagans' abominations. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_033.cfm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary blames the people around him for his evil. It says his name became a byword for infamy in Jewish records. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-33.html

**v. 3:** Guzik says Manasseh undid Hezekiah's reforms. He takes this to show that repentance, reform and revival don't last on their own. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/2-chronicles/2-chronicles-33.cfm
- Guzik cites Payne: worship of the stars ("host of heaven") goes back to Moses' day but was especially an Assyrian–Babylonian sin, tied to astrology. He cites Spurgeon: even Ahab hadn't worshipped the stars, and Manasseh brought in new worship from Assyria and Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- An exegetical note on Bible Hub says vv. 1–9 match 2 Kings 21:1–9 almost word for word. Chronicles strengthens some terms, for example by using the plurals "Baals" and "Asherahs." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/33-1.htm

**vv. 4–5:** Guzik's summary says Manasseh turned the temple itself into an idolatrous "brothel" devoted to Asherah. It quotes Spurgeon: he kept repeating his sins and making each worse. After one idol he set up a fouler one, and after altars in the temple courts he went further still. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/

**v. 6:** The Pulpit Commentary (Whitelaw) works out that Amon was born when Manasseh was about 45. It suggests this may mean more than one son was "passed through the fire." Clarkson takes the sorcery and witchcraft to show that sin clouds the mind as well as degrading the soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- A Precept Austin excerpt lists sexually explicit pagan altars, witchcraft and child sacrifice among his worst acts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-33-commentary

**v. 7:** The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge notes that the Aramaic Targum says Manasseh set up an image of himself in the sanctuary. It also notes that 2 Kings calls it "a graven image of the grove," that is, of Asherah/Astarte. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tsk/2-chronicles-33.html

**v. 8:** Guzik says the people ignored God's generous promises of protection for the obedient. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/

**v. 9:** Guzik says the people let themselves be led astray. He quotes Patterson and Austel: the nation's response to Hezekiah's reforms had been shallow, and without a strong godly leader they slid back quickly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- The Pulpit Commentary counts leading others into sin among the worst sins. Clarkson draws the lesson that one sinful person can do a world of harm. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says Manasseh's influence carried the whole nation into idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-33.html

**v. 10:** Guzik calls God's warning a great mercy: God owed no warning and could have judged at once. His patience wasn't weakness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- Whitelaw says the warnings showed God's patience and his wish that they repent, citing 1 Timothy 1:16 and 2 Peter 3:15. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html

**v. 11:**
- **Which king:** Gill names Esarhaddon, and says Jewish reckoning puts this in Manasseh's 22nd year. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/33-11.html Matthew Henry also mentions the "22nd year" tradition. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_033.cfm The Pulpit Commentary says Esarhaddon (about 680 BC), or less likely his son Ashurbanipal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- **Matches the Assyrian records (Whitelaw):** Assyrian inscriptions of both kings list "Manasseh king of Judah" as paying tribute. Leading him off with hooks and fetters fits pictures on the monuments. He was taken to Babylon because both kings called themselves "King of Assyria and Babylon" and lived there part of the year. Giving him back his throne fits Esarhaddon's known mildness toward rulers who submitted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- **Why Babylon:** Guzik quotes Selman, who says Babylon was under direct Assyrian control at the time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- A Bible Hub Q&A claims archaeology confirms that Assyrians used nose-hooks on royal captives. https://biblehub.com/q/Significance_of_Manasseh_s_repentance.htm
- Matthew Henry says Manasseh, already bound by his own sins, was now bound in chains. Hardship that God puts to good use often leads people to turn back to him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_033.cfm

**v. 12:** Guzik says "humbled" shows that pride was the root of Manasseh's sin. "God of his fathers" shows him returning to Hezekiah's faith, which Guzik links to Proverbs 22:6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- Matthew Henry says that, unlike Ahaz, Manasseh didn't sin more in his distress but humbled himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_033.cfm

**v. 13:** One older commentary on Bible Hub pictures Manasseh cut off from his bad advisers, confessing, and coming to know God as one who saves. From then on he lived a new life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/33-1.htm
- **The Pulpit Commentary (Whitelaw):**
  - Manasseh came to know God because he experienced God's mercy. Whitelaw's lesson: people only truly know God once they've received his mercy in Christ.
  - That knowledge came as the result of his repentance, not its cause.
  - His recovery rested only on God's grace, not on any merit.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- **On Precept Austin:** Henry is quoted saying no great sinner should despair, citing 1 Timothy 1:16. Another writer calls Manasseh "the Saul of the Old Testament," meaning God can save the worst sinner, but only through repentance and faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-33-commentary
- Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: the repentance is the Chronicler's main point, and the sins are the backdrop. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/

**v. 14:** Guzik says that before repenting Manasseh cared little for Judah's defence; afterwards he cared deeply. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/

**v. 15:** Guzik quotes Selman: each item removed here matches something in vv. 3 and 7, so this is a deliberate reversal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- Whitelaw says the change in his behaviour proved his conversion was real. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html

**v. 16:** Guzik's 2 Kings 21 study says removing idols and commanding Judah to serve the LORD proved the repentance was genuine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-21/
- Precept Austin notes that Manasseh once ordered idolatry and now orders faithfulness to God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-33-commentary

**v. 17:** Precept Austin's own comment: only Manasseh repented, not all of Judah, so the healing was personal, not national. It adds that outward reform doesn't wipe out deep-set habits, and a king's repentance can't change the people's hearts for them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-33-commentary
- Clarkson in the Pulpit Commentary calls this a serious drawback: Manasseh couldn't fully undo what he had done. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- Guzik says the reforms came too late to undo 55 years of damage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/

**v. 18:** Guzik says the Chronicler must have used sources with more information than 2 Kings, which doesn't mention the repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- A Bible Hub Q&A says the outside source shows the Chronicler chose from a fuller record to show that even the worst king wasn't beyond mercy. https://biblehub.com/q/2_Chron_33_18_on_Manasseh_s_repentance.htm
- Matthew Henry finds it strange that Kings doesn't mention the repentance. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-33-commentary

**v. 19:** Guzik's text (NKJV) gives the source as "the sayings of Hozai." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- GotQuestions says the Bible records that Manasseh prayed but doesn't give the prayer's words. https://www.gotquestions.org/Prayer-of-Manasseh.html

**v. 20:**
- **Guzik's reading:**
  - Because Manasseh truly repented, it's fitting that he "rested with his fathers."
  - He quotes Selman: Manasseh's turnaround explains why the exile didn't come in his reign, and he illustrates God's promise in 2 Chronicles 7.
  - He links Manasseh's arrest to the revolts under Ashurbanipal (652–648 BC).
  - He quotes Spurgeon: while this story stands, no one can rightly despair of being forgiven.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- A Bible Hub Q&A says the reforms put off Judah's judgment for nearly half a century. https://biblehub.com/q/Significance_of_Manasseh_s_repentance.htm

**vv. 21–22:** Clarkson says Amon, at 22, chose evil on purpose and lacked his father's excuse of youth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-33.html
- Matthew Henry answers those who take Amon's wickedness as proof Manasseh never truly repented: many good kings had wicked sons. He does suggest one failing, though. Manasseh threw out the images but didn't destroy them as Deuteronomy 7:5 requires, which left them for Amon. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_033.cfm
- The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge makes the same point. It adds that this didn't affect Manasseh's eternal state. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tsk/2-chronicles-33.html

**v. 23:** Guzik quotes Trapp citing Glycas: Amon planned to sin like his father and repent later, and was cut off for that presumption. He also quotes Selman: Manasseh and Amon both show that fatalism about God's judgment is wrong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says Manasseh's case is in the Bible so an old sinner won't despair, and Amon's case is beside it so the young won't put off repenting. It warns against turning grace into a trap. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-33.html

**v. 24:** Guzik says a palace plot like this belongs more to the northern kingdom's story. He quotes Patterson and Austel, who suggest a power struggle between factions loyal to Assyria and those against it, during the revolts of 642–639 BC. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/

**v. 25:** Guzik sees a hopeful sign: after about 57 years of wicked kings, the people finally acted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-33/
- He quotes Dilday: Amon's only good contribution was fathering one of Judah's best kings, Josiah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/2-chronicles/2-chronicles-33.cfm

---

### Where traditions differ (vv. 18–19: the "Prayer of Manasseh")
The verses mention a prayer, and a later text claims to be that prayer. Traditions treat it differently:
- **Protestant (evangelical):** GotQuestions says Jews, Catholics and Protestants all treat it as non-canonical, probably written under a false name. It notes the prayer later appeared in the Matthew, Geneva and King James Bibles. It objects that the prayer says Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did not sin. https://www.gotquestions.org/Prayer-of-Manasseh.html
- **Lutheran and Anglican printings:** A Cyclopedia entry on StudyLight says Luther put it last among the Apocrypha. The Matthew Bible, then the Bishops' Bible and the Authorized (King James) Version, placed it among the Apocrypha too. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/m/manasses-the-prayer-of.html
- **Wesley Center:** describes it as a prayer of sorrow for sin "placed on the lips" of Manasseh to fill the gap left by vv. 12–19. https://wesley.nnu.edu/sermons-essays-books/noncanonical-literature/noncanonical-literature-ot-apocrypha/prayer-of-manasseh/
- **Matthew Henry** calls it a good and fitting prayer from the apocryphal books. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-33-commentary

### Other views
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says the prayer is based on vv. 11–13, and that v. 18 points to lost records. The official Clementine Vulgate put it in an appendix. The article says it reads as Christian in spirit and may not be Jewish in origin. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01601a.htm
- **Orthodox:** The OCA says that for the Orthodox the prayer is part of the Bible, and it is used in the Great Compline service. https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/doctrine-scripture/old-testament/wisdom
- **Older scholarship:** Swete's *Introduction to the Old Testament in Greek* says it is usually seen as a Greek-speaking Jew's attempt to recreate the prayer of v. 18. https://ccel.org/ccel/swete/greekot/greekot.iv.ii.html
